analysis.one_liner: Requires trucks and large trailers to carry rear, side, and front underride guards that stop cars from sliding underneath in crashes.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and never received a committee markup or floor vote before the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: When a car collides with a large truck, the car can slide underneath the trailer, shearing off the roof and killing the people inside — an 'underride' crash. This bill would have required the Department of Transportation to set rules requiring rear, side, and front underride guards on trailers and large trucks, tested so they prevent a car's cabin from being crushed at 35 miles per hour. It also required drivers to inspect the guards for rust, cracked welds, and loose fasteners before trips, set up an advisory committee including family members of crash victims, and ordered quarterly public reporting of underride crash victim data.
analysis.who_benefits: People driving passenger cars, and their families. Hundreds of people die in underride crashes each year, many of them preventable with guards strong enough to keep a car's passenger compartment from being crushed. The bill also gave crash victims' families a formal seat in the rulemaking process and created public, quarterly reporting of underride crash victim data.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Car occupants and crash victims' families

how_it_helps.text: Requires rear, side, and front underride guards on trailers, semi-trailers, and large single-unit trucks, with a performance standard that guards must prevent intrusion into a passenger car's cabin in 35 mph crash tests at full, 50%, and 30% overlap.
Requires drivers to pre-trip inspect underride protection systems for rusted metal, cracked welds, and missing or loose fasteners, and complete repairs before operating.

Establishes a Committee on Underride Protection to oversee rulemaking, including at least four members whose families were affected by underride crashes, and requires DOT to publish quarterly data on underride crash victims on a public website.
The bill is dedicated to named victims of underride crashes and cites NHTSA reporting of hundreds of preventable fatalities and NTSB recommendations for all three guard types.

analysis.who_pays: Trucking companies and trailer manufacturers, who bear the cost of manufacturing, installing, and maintaining the guards, and indirectly consumers through freight prices. Carriers and shippers would also face added inspection and repair obligations on every affected vehicle.

drawbacks.text: The equipment is not free: carriers must manufacture, install, and maintain guards on every affected trailer and truck, and added guard weight can reduce payload capacity, which would show up in freight costs. Small carriers with older fleets would face proportionally larger retrofit burdens.

Side underride guards in particular have drawn objections from the trucking industry on cost and on the added weight they place on trailers, which industry groups argue can affect trailer durability and payload — a cost honest supporters of the bill would acknowledge.
The bill sets a fixed 35 mph performance standard written into statute, which gives the safety agency limited flexibility to adapt the standard as testing and technology evolve.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is preventing a specific, grisly, and largely survivable-if-avoided category of death: a car sliding under a trailer and having its passenger compartment crushed. The costs fall on a concentrated industry and pass partly to consumers through freight prices. The tradeoff is favorable on safety grounds, though the statutory 35 mph standard and fixed deadlines leave regulators less room to tune requirements than a pure agency rulemaking would.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee on the day it was introduced, then sent to its Highways and Transit Subcommittee, where it sat without a markup or a vote until the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Steve Cohen introduced the Stop Underrides Act on March 8, 2021, with 23 original cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure.
The committee never held a markup; the bill was referred to the Subcommittee on Highways and Transit the day after introduction and no further action was taken.
The bill accumulated 24 cosponsors, all Democrats, and died at the end of the 117th Congress without ever reaching the House floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Truck and trailer manufacturers and motor carriers are better off because the bill died, since they avoid equipment, maintenance, and inspection costs. Families of underride crash victims remain without the mandated protections.

for.name: Rep. Steve Cohen
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee.

for.name: 24 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all 24 cosponsors were Democrats.

against.name: Chair Peter DeFazio and House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to the Highways and Transit Subcommittee and never scheduled a markup, so the bill never advanced.

against.name: American Trucking Associations and trucking industry groups
against.what_they_did: Opposed mandatory side underride guard requirements, citing equipment costs and added trailer weight.

sides.party_line_note: All 24 cosponsors were Democrats, and the Democratic chairman of the committee of referral never advanced the bill; no Republican support is recorded.

industries.note: The bill would require them to build and certify rear, side, and front underride guards meeting a 35 mph crash-test standard on new trailers and large trucks. Their avoidance of these compliance costs runs against the public's interest in stronger crash protection.

Carriers would bear equipment, pre-trip inspection, periodic inspection, and repair obligations on every affected vehicle, and added guard weight can reduce payload. The industry's interest in avoiding those costs runs against public safety gains.

industries.industry: Underride guard and safety equipment makers
industries.note: A federal mandate for three types of guards would create a guaranteed market for guard manufacturers, and the bill directs DOT to solicit prototype designs for high-capacity barriers.

Fewer catastrophic underride fatalities would mean fewer large injury claims, but the bill also adds inspection and repair obligations carriers must document. The industry gets a seat on the underride protection committee.
